title: Inside the 6R80 Automatic Transmission
introduction:
I use these exploded drawings as a mechanical family tree: find the assembly, follow its bracket, then trace an individual part’s callout to the table. The Item column connects drawing to description; the Part Number column supplies the corresponding identifier. Keep the description alongside that identifier, especially where similar seals, bearings and retaining rings appear throughout the transmission.

Start at the torque converter and pump in the upper drawing, then follow the separated clutch assemblies and gear components. The repeating stacks of friction and steel plates become much less bewildering once the drawing spreads them out for you. Notice the table’s distinction between internally and externally splined plates, and between a complete assembly and a component described as part of that assembly. Those distinctions help you understand what belongs together.

The torque converter provides the fluid connection between engine and transmission. Inside the transmission, clutches establish relationships between members of the planetary gearsets; those relationships produce different ratios. The valve body handles hydraulic control, turning commanded changes into routed fluid pressure. It is a different assembly from the gears themselves.

This reference covers the 6R80. Match model-dependent entries to the fitted transmission rather than counting the plates or fasteners drawn. Use the illustrations and table for identification and assembly relationships; they do not establish removal order, clearances, tightening specifications, seal installation methods or fastener reuse rules.

edits.why: I start with the long assembly brackets, then follow each smaller callout to the matching table entry. The dashed centerlines help connect separated components across the drawing. Their spacing makes small parts visible; it does not represent an installed clearance or authorize a disassembly sequence. Where a callout needs further identification, use its matching legend entry rather than guessing from its shape.

edits.text: Finding Components in the Transmission Cutaway
edits.why: I use this drawing like a transparent gearbox casing: it makes the crowded arrangement easier to understand without pretending the parts are accessible from outside. Start at the large rounded torque converter on the left, then look immediately behind it for the front pump assembly. Continue along the central shaft to locate the clutch packs and planetary gearing. The front planetary gearset and the forward and overdrive clutches have their own entries in the accompanying location table. Follow the illustration's numbered leader lines to their endpoints, then match the callouts to that table; the lines belong to the illustration. The lower part of the cutaway shows the control assembly above the fluid pan. The valve body routes and regulates hydraulic pressure, while the planetary gearsets provide different ratios as their members are driven or held. Keep the detailed disassembled-view parts table separate from this location key: each numbering scheme belongs to its own illustration. In the parts table, retain distinctions such as seal color, internally versus externally splined plates, select-fit pieces and model-dependent components. Those labels distinguish parts; they do not supply fit-selection measurements or establish interchangeability. Use this reference to identify components and understand their arrangement. It does not provide a removal sequence, clutch application chart, hydraulic flow map or service specifications.
